- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative or neutral (≤0.33), model often overcorrects downward; allow slight upward bias or avoid sharp declines.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” buffer or reduce forecast slope for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment shifts from positive to negative (or vice versa), model often lags; adjust forecast to align with sentiment change within 1–2 days.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 85–88), model tends to hold high forecasts; reduce forecast by 2–5% per day until reversion stabilizes.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the period (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is bullish; apply a “sentiment decay” factor to dampen initial forecast rise.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “1.00” (strong bullish) followed by “0.00” (neutral), model often fails to adjust; introduce a “sentiment decay” rule to reduce forecast by 1–2% per day after sentiment drops.
